newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia welcomes ratings for forthcoming Eurobond.
newsitem.headline: Russia welcomes ratings for forthcoming Eurobond.

text.p: Russia welcomed the better-than-expected credit ratings it received from three agencies which pave the way for its first foreign bond since before the 1917 Bolshevik revolution, Finance Minister Alexander Livshits said Monday.
"This is real money, this is quick money and it is quite big money," Livshits told a news conference.
Moody's assigned a Ba2 ceiling for Russia's long-term foreign-currency bonds, Standard & Poors gave a BB minus rating and IBCA gave a BB plus rating.
The rating provides guidance for foreign investors considering buying the Eurobonds, or bonds denominated in European currencies, Russia intends to issue this year.
None of the three ratings is investment grade -- the level at which conservative pension funds can invest -- but they were better than expected.

"They are below investment grade, which means there is an element of doubt in the stability of the political and economic course, which means that if something happens Russia could default," said a senior official, who asked not to be identified.
But Livshits said the ratings meant investors felt Russia's ecomomy was moving in the right direction.
"It is quite a high rating," he said. "It is a respectable rating. It means world investors have long-term confidence in Russian paper."
Hungary, Mexico, India, Slovakia has similar ratings while Turkey, Venezuela and Brazil were lower, he said.
Russia would issue the Eurobond by the end of the year, he said.
"I do not think the first issue will be a massive one, despite our budget problems, but for us prospects on the market are more important than immediate sums of money," he said.
Livshits said the Eurobond would have a longer maturity than securities now circulating on the domestic market.
The longest paper on the domestic market is a two-year government bond.
London bankers expect the first Eurobond will be for between $300 millionand $500 million with a three to five-year maturity.
According to the draft 1997 budget, Russia is planning to raise $1.3 billion in Eurobonds next year.
Russia has removed hurdles to the Eurobond issue by negotiating agreements to reschedule its debts with the London Club of creditor banks and Paris Club of government creditors.
It may soon join the Paris Club as a creditor now that some countries, which owe about $35 billion to Russia, have signed agreements with the International Monetary Fund, Livshits said.
Under the stand-by agreements with the IMF, these countries must settle their international debts.
